student_profile.student_background: Practicing healthcare professionals across roles — clinicians, nurses, allied health staff, administrators, and researchers — non-technical, no programming assumed. Mixed comfort and confidence with AI tools.
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Experienced adult professionals with strong domain readiness.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Wide variation in informatics fluency; assume no prior training in health data standards. Learners engage best with REAL record examples — actual note text, lab values with their metadata, imaging headers — not abstract definitions. Plain language, terms defined on first use, short daily sessions.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: This module teaches HEALTHCARE DATA as the foundation for AI in healthcare, and it is structured EXACTLY as four learning objectives, in this fixed order: (1) map the major healthcare data sources; (2) distinguish structured from unstructured data; (3) recognize data quality and interoperability issues; (4) apply ethical and governance frameworks. The module's framing line is: AI is only as good as the data behind it — knowing the data is knowing what AI can and cannot do. AI itself appears only as brief context (data is what any downstream tool consumes; data quality bounds tool reliability), never as a session's subject. Every named fact, definition, standard, and example MUST come from the provided source excerpts; never invent an example, statistic, or citation. Where the sources do not cover a named subtopic (for example omics data, patient-generated data, administrative claims data, or a specific consent regulation), either describe it generically in one sentence or omit it — NEVER invent specifics for it. When citing a named source or standard, its URL from the excerpts appears on the slide.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Visual-first, punchy slides modeled on the client's own decks — NEVER walls of bullets. Most slides carry ONE idea in at most 30 words of body text: a big statement, a short quoted dialogue, a figure with a two-line explanation, or a compact table. Directly under each frame title, put a one-line italic message stating the slide's takeaway. When a figure from the source excerpts fits the slide, the figure DOMINATES the slide with at most two short lines of text beside or below it. The lecture script carries the depth; the slides carry the punch. Open every session with a real hook from the sources; close every session with a knowledge check.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Assess data literacy per objective: naming where a given piece of clinical data lives, telling structured from unstructured data and why it matters for AI, spotting a quality or interoperability problem in a record fragment, and identifying the governance question a data reuse raises. No exams, no coding.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: By the end of this module, learners will be able to: (1) map the major healthcare data sources — what each contains and how it is stored; (2) distinguish structured from unstructured data — lab values versus free-text notes, and why the proportion matters for AI development; (3) recognize data quality and interoperability issues — missingness, coding inconsistency, FHIR, OMOP, and why hospitals struggle to share data; (4) apply ethical and governance frameworks — consent, de-identification, secondary use, and data ownership in research and AI training.
course_structure.total_number_of_weeks: 1 module of EXACTLY 4 sessions — one session per learning objective, equal length
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline: The module has EXACTLY FOUR sessions, one per learning objective, in this fixed order — the syllabus must not merge, split, add, or reorder them. Session 1 — Map the major healthcare data sources: what the medical record is (legal record, designated record set, EHR); one patient, many systems — where clinical data lives (EHR, laboratory, pharmacy, imaging archive/PACS); what each source contains and how it is stored, taught through real record artifacts from the excerpts (a record-set definition, an imaging archive's workflow, a medication entry); other source types the excerpts do not cover (omics, patient-generated, administrative) named only generically in passing. Session 2 — Distinguish structured from unstructured data: lab values and coded entries versus free-text clinical notes; what coding a value buys (LOINC for laboratory observations, RxNorm for medications, normalized names and identifiers); what free text carries that codes do not (the documentation fundamentals of good notes); why the structured/unstructured proportion matters for any downstream tool. Session 3 — Recognize data quality and interoperability issues: why the same clinical data can look different in two systems; coding inconsistency and missingness taught through record fragments; how exchange standards address it — FHIR resources and profiles for exchange, OMOP common data model for research; DICOM as the imaging interchange standard; why hospitals still struggle to share data. Session 4 — Apply ethical and governance frameworks: what the excerpts support on consent, de-identification, secondary use, and data ownership — the record as a legal document and the duty of documentation; releasing and protecting the record (designated record set decisions); data protection by design in research data models (limiting identifying details); open-science reuse of observational data. This session teaches ONLY what the provided sources support and stays shorter rather than inventing regulatory content the excerpts lack.

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Per-session knowledge checks (3 questions, answers on the following slide). Record Reading — given a real fragment, identify its source system, whether it is structured, what quality issue it shows, or what governance question it raises.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Short applied checks inside each deck; self-paced.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Institution-approved learning platform; accessibility standards; no patient-identifiable information. Named tools, studies, and standards are permitted when drawn from the provided public sources with attribution.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Facilitator-led or self-paced; no teaching assistant assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Professional development; each session is a self-paced ~45-minute module tied to one learning objective. All four sessions must be of comparable length so each objective receives equal reading time.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Aligns with the digital-education program's goals for health-data literacy and responsible use of clinical information systems.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: All named examples, statistics, and cases must be traceable to the provided public sources (attribution on slide); no fabricated content; no patient-identifiable information.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Module must include learning outcomes, the four-session structure (one session per objective), the assessment approach, and a sources page listing every cited source with its URL.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: Revision after client review: the previous version organized content BY SOURCE (one section per standard), which read as disorganized. The client's own lecture materials structure a session as ORDERED LEARNING OBJECTIVES, with the standards woven in where they serve an objective (FHIR and OMOP belong under data quality and interoperability, not as standalone sections). Equal reading time per objective was an explicit client request.

session_structure: Each chapter of this course IS one session and covers exactly ONE of the four learning objectives, in the fixed order given. Every session: opens with a slide stating its objective in the client's phrasing plus a real hook from the sources; is built AROUND worked record examples (at most a third of slides purely conceptual); closes with a knowledge check of exactly 3 questions (answers on the following slide). 18-24 slides per session, hard cap 30; all four sessions comparable in length.
engagement_style: ONE THING PER SLIDE — every slide holds exactly one definition-in-use, one worked record example, one table, or one question; never combine two ideas. (1) THE FIRST CONTENT SLIDE after the title states the session's learning objective and its takeaway line, then the next slide is a real record moment from the excerpts — never an abstract framework. (2) WORKED RECORD EXAMPLES are the backbone — 3-5 per session, each on its OWN slide: show a small real record fragment or value from the excerpts, ask what a careful reader must know, then walk what the source, structure, standard, or governance rule adds. (3) Session 1 includes one 'One patient, many systems' TABLE slide: rows = data types (notes, labs, imaging, medications), columns = where it lives and how it is stored (rendered with the LaTeX colorbox command as short chips). (4) Session 2 includes one slide contrasting THE SAME clinical fact as a coded entry versus as note text, built from excerpt material. (5) Session 3 includes one worked interoperability example: the same data element represented differently in two systems, and what the exchange standard does about it. (6) Session 4 includes one PROVENANCE-AND-PERMISSION questions slide: the questions a careful reader asks about origin, purpose, transformation, and permission to reuse — phrased as questions, drawn from the excerpts. (7) Each session includes ONE discussion-cases slide: 3-4 numbered one-line judgment scenarios with no clean answer, tied to that session's objective. (8) TONE: slide titles are active and curiosity-driven, never bureaucratic. (9) REGISTER: the audience is practicing clinicians and healthcare staff — never the words 'students' or 'textbook'. (10) VISUALS: use ONLY real figures present in the retrieved excerpts, each on its own slide (0.75+ textwidth, at most two short lines of text). (11) When a slide cites a named standard, article, or organization, put its SOURCE URL from the excerpts at the bottom. (12) NEVER invent a named example, number, quote, or citation — if it is not in the excerpts, teach it generically or leave it out. (13) AI appears on at most 2 slides per session, as context only (the framing line: AI is only as good as the data behind it), never as a slide's subject.
